column1: # crypt(5) password hash algorithms, keyed on the $id$ marker.
# severity is how the hash itself scores - a strong algorithm is OK, a weak one is a finding
# no matter whose account it is. hashcat/john name the cracking mode so a learner can go
# straight from "I found a hash" to "here is how you would attack it".
# id   algo                    severity  hashcat  john             description

column6: 13-character legacy hash with an 8-character password limit. Falls to a GPU almost instantly - it should not exist on a modern system.
Old and fast. A commodity GPU tries billions per second, so treat every $1$ hash as already cracked if the password is at all common.
Blowfish-based adaptive hash. Strong; only genuinely weak passwords fall in reasonable time.
bcrypt (2b), the current OpenBSD default. Strong.
SHA-256 crypt. Respectable, but noticeably softer against GPUs than SHA-512 or yescrypt.
The long-standing Linux default. Strong when the password is; the round count still matters.
The modern default on Debian 11+, Ubuntu 22.04+ and current Arch. Memory-hard and strong. hashcat has no native mode yet - crack with john --format=yescrypt.
yescrypt with the GOST hash. Strong; crack with john.
SHA-1 based crypt. Weak by modern standards.
A bare MD5 marker rather than $1$ crypt. Very weak; usually a sign of an application hash that leaked into a system file.
